slideText: Apo, the peace of our islands changed one day in 1521
when strangers with sails appeared on our shores. They were Spaniards.
They were led by Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese explorer sailing for Spain.
He was looking for a way to reach the Spice Islands.
When they landed in Cebu, they met Rajah Humabon.
He welcomed them, curious about the newcomers and their strange religion.
Magellan baptized Rajah Humabon, his wife, and hundreds of others.
They were promised protection and friendship under one god.
In Mactan, there lived a brave chieftain named Lapu-Lapu.
He refused to kneel to any foreign king.
Magellan tried to force Lapu-Lapu to submit. But Lapu-Lapu stood his ground.
They fought fiercely on the beach. Magellan fell that day.
Magellan's men left in defeat. For a time, our islands were free again.
But Spain did not forget.
Spain kept trying to come back. It took more than 40 years
before they succeeded in returning and staying for good.
In 1565, Miguel Lopez de Legazpi arrived from Mexico.
He brought soldiers, priests, and orders to build a colony.
To win trust, Legazpi made a sanduguan, a blood compact, with Datu Sikatuna of Bohol.
It was a sign of friendship but also a strategy.
Legazpi then went to Cebu but did not just visit. He fought and took it by force.
A settlement was built where the old kingdom stood.
Further north in Manila, Rajah Sulayman resisted. He warned the Spaniards:
'I will not be a friend to anyone who comes to conquer.'
There was a battle. Our warriors fought with spears and bravery
but the Spaniards had guns and cannons. Manila fell.
In 1571, Legazpi made Manila the capital of the Spanish East Indies.
From here, the Spaniards would rule the islands.
They began building forts and churches, not just with wood, but with rules:
Spanish rules, Spanish gods, Spanish laws.
Some datus made peace with Spain, hoping to protect their people.
Others were forced, tricked, or defeated.
Life began to change. Old customs were questioned.
New ways were taught. Some were accepted, others resisted.
Resistance never fully stopped. In the mountains, forests, and distant islands,
many refused to bow down.
Never forget those who stood firm, apo. Lapu-Lapu, Sulayman, and many unnamed
heroes showed us that freedom is worth fighting for.
So began the long chapter of Spanish rule.
Not by peace alone, but also through war, clever alliances, and resistance.

slideText: When Spain finally settled on our islands, they didn't just bring swords.
They brought rulers, priests, and rules.
One of the first systems they set up was called the Encomienda.
The king gave land to a Spaniard, who became an encomendero.
But it wasn't just land. The encomendero also collected tributes like
food, gold, or labor from the people living there.
They were supposed to protect the natives and teach them the faith.
But some became greedy, treating people unfairly.
Then came the Reduccion. Spaniards forced scattered villages
to move into town centers, to make ruling and converting easier.
These new towns had a central plaza, a church, and government buildings.
It was the Spanish way of organizing life.
They chose a local leader called the gobernadorcillo to govern the town.
But he had to follow Spanish orders.
Religion became a powerful tool. Friars taught the people Catholic prayers,
banned native rituals, and held great power in town.
There were many religious orders like Augustinians, Franciscans, Dominicans,
Jesuits each with missions in different provinces.
Some friars were kind. But others acted like kings.
They punished people, interfered in politics, and owned vast lands.
They built schools too. Boys studied in seminaries, girls in convents.
But most people only learned to read for prayers.
People were also forced to work. They built roads, churches, and ships
under the polo y servicio that forced labor for men.
Every family paid tribute. Those who failed were punished.
Some families ran to the mountains to escape.
A few native leaders became part of the Principalia.
They gained privileges and helped enforce Spanish control.
Sometimes, friars and government officials clashed.
But in the end, they both wanted control.
Over time, mestizos children of mixed Spanish and native blood
became a growing group. Some rose to wealth and power.
Though the friars walked among us, and many people converted, some kept their old
beliefs in secret. The spirit of our ancestors never fully disappeared.
Life under Spain seemed quiet.
But under that silence were seeds of anger, waiting to grow.
These were the tools of control like coins, crosses, and records.
Spain ruled not just with weapons, but with systems.
Now you know, apo, how they ruled us. Not only through conquest,
but by changing how we lived, prayed, and worked.

slideText: Every year, they paid more for gold, crops, and labor.
Eventually, the people said, 'Sobra na.' And they began to resist.
Even in the beginning, there was tension. In 1574,
Lakandula and Sulayman led a revolt when Spain broke their agreement.
The revolt failed. Like many after it.
But it showed that the people would not simply bow forever.
In 1587, GABRIELA SILANG wasn't born yet, but brave women already stood up.
Like Magalat in Cagayan and Tamblot in Bohol.
Tamblot, a babaylan, led a revolt in 1621.
He wanted to return to native beliefs. Religion was his weapon.
Many revolts were spiritual. People were forced to abandon their gods.
Some obeyed. Others fought back.
Bankaw had welcomed the Spaniards years before.
But by 1621, he saw their true colors and revolted too.
In Pangasinan, a man named Malong tried to build his own kingdom in 1660.
He was once part of the system until he rebelled.
Soon after, Juan Caragay and the Zambals joined.
The flames of resistance kept spreading.
And finally, in the north, came a woman named Gabriela Silang.
After her husband Diego was killed, she took up his cause.
She led one of the fiercest uprisings in Ilocos, hoping to build a free land.
But she was captured and hanged.
Even when revolts failed, some rebels fled to the hills.
There, they lived free, beyond Spain's reach.
Spanish priests and officials feared these uprisings.
They wrote about the 'restless' natives in their reports.
To calm things down, Spain started educating some natives.
But it wasn't out of kindness and it was to create loyal allies.
Many rebels believed in anting-anting charms that would protect them.
Their revolts were also acts of faith.
Revolt after revolt, the leaders were captured and punished.
Heads were displayed, to scare the rest.
But the people never forgot. The pain became stories.
The stories became anger. And the anger never truly died.
Even in silence, the people planned.
Revolts would continue bigger, stronger, more united.
These are not just places. They are the cradle of our courage.
Each revolt added to our fight for freedom.
Remember their names, apo. They stood when others bowed.
Even if they are lost, their spirit lives in us.
